newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Britain's Thor pays out in S. African mercury case.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Thor pays out in S. African mercury case.

text.p: Britain's Thor Chemicals Holdings Ltd on Friday reached a 9.4 million rand ($2.1 million) settlement with 20 workers who say they suffered mercury poisoning at the company's South African plant, a lawyer said.

"Today my clients have accepted the total offer of a 9.4 million rand settlement for damages and costs from the parent company in the United Kingdom," Richard Meeran, representing the workers and their families, told a news conference.
He accused Thor of exploiting the health of workers at the Cato Ridge chemical plant in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province where toxic mercury catalyst waste products were recycled.
"The only recycling Thor did was of workers who were sent to work in the gardens or laid off when the level of mercury in their blood and urine reached a certain level," Meeran said.
"In that way they avoided implementing proper working practices," Meeran said.

Cowley, questioned in London, said the settlement did not mean the company acknowledged blame. It was more cost efficient to settle the case out of court than pay for court costs even if the company won.
"It is a commercial settlement which comes out of the legal aid situation in the United Kingdom," he told Reuters.

"If the case had gone to conclusion and we had won we would have still had something like five million pounds ($8.12 million) costs which we would have been unable to recover as the plaintiffs are legal aided and legal aid refuses to pay the cost of a successful defence," he added.
The company has admitted that three workers at the Cato Ridge facility took ill after mercury vapour entered their breathing apparatus. Two died later and a third suffers from neurological problems.
Meeran said another 17 workers had been affected to varying degrees and this had formed the basis of the legal action against Thor.
Cowley said the company does not accept that the 17 remaining defendants suffered from mercury poisoning.
The South African plant still manufactures chemical products but has been instructed by the government to cease its mercury operations pending an investigation.
A presidential commission is investigating ways of getting rid of 3,000 tonnes of mercury waste products stored in corroding drums on the plant.
The first phase of the two phase probe has been completed and the findings sent to President Nelson Mandela, but they have not yet been made public. ($1=.6161 Pound) ($ = 4.455 South African Rand)
